title: The classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey sets
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: OpenAI's classification (2026) of the finite Euclidean Ramsey sets: a finite set A with affine span R^d is Ramsey exactly when a matrix P over B = F (x)_Q F, F the field generated by the coordinates, satisfies (p_i (x) 1)^T P (1 (x) p_i) = 0 at every point and has multiplied spatial block I_d. The course proves the equivalence with a tensor condition on affine functions; necessity by a colouring with (2s+1)^s colours built from Q-linear functionals; a finite lattice identity through Laurent polynomials, logarithmic coordinates and the flatness of completion; two-scale configurations by Gaussian smoothing, discretization and rational approximation; the Hales-Jewett theorem by colour focusing; ultrafilter semigroups, Ellis's idempotent and the corner group; a path criterion in a free group; and the correction of endpoints through the derived series of the kernel of the exponent sum, with averaging over coordinate permutations. Consequences: subsets of finite transitive sets and all sets of at most five concyclic points are Ramsey; the kites K_a with transcendental a are Ramsey and, by a theorem of Leader, Russell and Walters proved in the course, embed in no finite transitive set; nine generic points of a circle and three squares rotated by a Liouville angle are not Ramsey.
prerequisites: linear algebra over a field, including Gaussian elimination and the diagonalization of real symmetric matrices; Zorn's lemma

the programme's course Commutative algebra for geometry (AG-CA): the Hilbert basis theorem (lesson Noetherian and Artinian rings, Theorem 2.1) and the flatness of completion (lesson Completion, Theorem 3.2), used in the third lesson

core courses Real Analysis I and II (Lebl, Basic Analysis I and II, version 6.3): Taylor's theorem (Theorem 4.3.2), the Leibniz integral rule (Theorem 9.1.1), Riemann integrability of continuous functions on rectangles (Theorem 10.1.15), Fubini's theorem (Theorem 10.2.2) and the change of variables (Theorem 10.7.2), used in the fourth lesson

checks.reading: The manuscript 'A classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026; build/main.tex and the sections introduction, tensors, stencil, pairs, paths, groups and consequences, 85 kB of TeX; local library copy openai-math-20261006) was read in full on 17 Oct 2026, and every step was derived again while the lessons were written. No error affecting a statement was found. Changes of form in the course: (1) results the manuscript cites are proved in the lessons: the Hales-Jewett theorem (fifth lesson, by colour focusing), compactness of the ultrafilter space, Ellis's idempotent and the corner group p(beta S)p (sixth lesson; the manuscript cites Hindman-Strauss and Ellis), the reduction to a finite dimension (seventh lesson, through a nonprincipal ultrafilter; the manuscript cites Erdős et al., Proposition 4, and includes a proof), Liouville's argument for the transcendence of the angle parameter, and the theorem of Leader, Russell and Walters that the kites K_a embed in no finite transitive set (last lesson, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2; the manuscript cites it). (2) For that theorem the proof of arXiv:1012.5468 (TeX source read) takes as well known that real representations of finite groups can be realized with algebraic entries, and passes to irreducible representations; the lesson obtains the algebraic coefficients of det L(alpha, beta) from Newton's identities, since the trace of a group element is a sum of roots of unity, and works with the fixed space of the group and its orthogonal complement. A slip in that proof ('there exists non-zero w' where 'no non-zero w' is meant, Lemma 4) is recorded in ERRATA_FOUND.md. (3) The flatness of completion and the Hilbert basis theorem come from the programme's AG-CA lessons (the manuscript cites Stacks Tag 00MB). (4) The Gaussian moments are derived from linear changes of variables and Fubini's theorem, with the normalizing constant kept as omega, the integral of exp(-t^2/2); the sphere matrix of the quadratic interpolation proposition is written out.
